c.tagline: The world's greatest open-air museum, where Karnak, the Valley of the Kings and Nile feluccas share one riverbank.

taxi.fareNote: Luxor taxis are unmetered—agree the fare before setting off; ride-hailing (Uber, Careem) exists but coverage is limited, so most visitors negotiate with taxis, hire a driver for the day, or cross the Nile by public ferry or felucca. Horse-drawn calèches ply the Corniche for short scenic rides (fix the price first).

emergency.note: 122 reaches the police and 123 the ambulance service; 126 is the tourist police. Response can be slow, and larger hotels can help arrange care.

avoid.reason: Persistent touts/hassle at the temples and on the Nile corniche — agree prices; otherwise safe

hood_desc: The Nile-side promenade on the east bank and the heart of Luxor's visitor scene, lined with grand hotels, cafes, cruise-boat moorings and calèche stands, steps from Luxor Temple and the museum; the convenient, scenic base for first-timers.

The lively streets around Luxor Temple and the covered Sharia al-Souk bazaar, full of spice, scarf, alabaster and souvenir stalls plus budget hotels and local eateries; atmospheric and central, right among the sights.

The quieter northern district built around the vast Karnak Temple complex, more residential and local than the tourist Corniche, with a few riverside resorts and easy access to the temple at opening time.

A rural village on the Nile's west bank directly across from town, reached by the public ferry, with palm groves, guesthouses and boutique hotels; a laid-back base close to the antiquities and far from the Corniche bustle.

The west-bank zone spread among the Valley of the Kings, Hatshepsut's temple, the Colossi of Memnon and Medinet Habu, dotted with small hotels and mud-brick guesthouses; best for travellers who want to wake among the tombs and catch dawn hot-air balloon flights.
lodging: Bob Marley House Sherief Hotel Luxor

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only; avoid ice from unknown sources.

transit.hours: Minibuses and microbuses run roughly 6am-10pm; the public Nile ferry between the East and West Banks and feluccas operate through the day, with taxis and calèches filling other trips.
transit.note: Luxor has no metro, tram or urban rail. Shared minibuses and microbuses cover town routes cheaply, a public ferry and feluccas cross the Nile to the West Bank antiquities, and taxis, calèches or ride-hailing apps handle most visitor trips.
transit.pay: Minibuses, the public ferry and feluccas are paid in cash to the driver or boatman; there is no transit card. Ride-hailing apps (Uber, Careem) are paid in-app or cash where available.

bus: Intercity coaches to Aswan, Hurghada & Cairo (Go Bus, Blue Bus)
ferry: Public ferry between the East and West Banks
train: Egyptian National Railways to Aswan, Cairo & Alexandria (incl. overnight sleeper trains)

transit.m: Taxi to the Corniche / East Bank (15-25 min)

tip.r: ~10% at restaurants; baksheesh (small tips) is customary and expected for many services—boatmen, guides, drivers and site staff.

food.name: Koshari
food.desc: Egypt's national comfort food: rice, lentils and macaroni layered with spiced tomato sauce, chickpeas, crisp fried onions and garlicky vinegar.

places.name: Sofra Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Restored 1930s house off Sharia Mohamed Farid; the standard reference for Egyptian home cooking here.

places.name: Al-Sahaby Lane Restaurant
places.note: Family-run since 1930, rooftop tables over the souq near the Avenue of Sphinxes.

places.name: Aboudi Coffee Break
places.note: Reliable, tourist-friendly cafe near the Nile with Egyptian staples and good coffee.

food.name: Molokhia
food.desc: Jute-leaf stew cooked to a green, silky texture with garlic and coriander, ladled over rice and eaten with chicken or rabbit.

places.name: Sofra Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Slow-cooked molokhia served with rice and chicken in a courtyard setting.

places.name: Al-Sahaby Lane Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing kitchen doing the classic Upper Egyptian version with rabbit or chicken.

places.name: Nubian House Restaurant
places.note: Traditional Nubian-style dining rooms across the river, good after a Valley of the Kings morning.

food.name: Tagen
food.desc: Not the Moroccan tagine but a stew baked in a small clay pot, usually lamb, beef or shrimp with tomato, onion and okra, served bubbling.

places.name: Sofra Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Best known dish on the menu; several tagen variations including okra and shrimp.

places.name: Al-Sahaby Lane Restaurant
places.note: Clay-pot stews alongside grills, with a shaded terrace for hot afternoons.

places.name: Nubian House Restaurant
places.note: Stone-oven cooking gives the tagen a deeper, smokier flavour.

food.name: Feteer meshaltet
food.desc: Paper-thin layered pastry folded with ghee and baked until flaky, served plain with honey and cheese or stuffed with meat and vegetables.

places.name: Sofra Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Sweet and savoury feteer made to order; good for sharing at breakfast or tea time.

places.name: Luxor Souq bakeries
places.note: Small bakeries in the covered market sell feteer by weight, straight from the oven.

places.name: Aboudi Coffee Break
places.note: Easy central option for feteer with honey and a coffee.

food.name: Hamam mahshi
food.desc: Pigeon stuffed with freekeh or spiced rice and roasted or grilled. A special-occasion dish across Upper Egypt, fiddly to eat and worth it.

places.name: Sofra Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Order ahead if possible; stuffed pigeon is a signature of the house.

places.name: Al-Sahaby Lane Restaurant
places.note: Grilled pigeon on the traditional menu alongside kofta and tagen.

places.name: 1886 Restaurant, Winter Palace
places.note: Formal dining room in the historic hotel for a dressed-up version; jacket preferred.

food.name: Taameya and foul
food.desc: Egyptian falafel made from split fava beans rather than chickpeas, fried green inside, plus slow-simmered foul medames. The universal breakfast.

places.name: Luxor Souq stalls
places.note: Morning stands frying taameya to order; cheapest and freshest before 10am.

places.name: Sofra Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Sit-down Egyptian breakfast spread with taameya, foul, salads and bread.

places.name: Aboudi Coffee Break
places.note: Central breakfast option with English-speaking staff and a printed menu.

food.name: Karkade
food.desc: Deep red hibiscus tea from Upper Egypt, served hot in winter and iced in summer. Tart, faintly floral and usually well sweetened.

places.name: Al-Sahaby Lane Restaurant
places.note: Widely praised hibiscus tea; a good place to sit out the midday heat.

places.name: Sofra Restaurant and Cafe
places.note: Often brings complimentary karkade with dessert; the courtyard is the spot.

places.name: Winter Palace terrace
places.note: Colonial-era hotel terrace overlooking the Nile for an iced karkade at sunset.

food.name: Sugarcane juice
food.desc: Asab: cane pressed to order into a cloudy, grassy-sweet green juice. Luxor sits in Egypt's sugarcane belt so it is everywhere and very cheap.

places.name: Station Street juice bars
places.note: Cluster of asab presses near the railway station; look for the stacked cane out front.

places.name: Luxor Souq juice stands
places.note: Pressed to order in front of you; ask for it without added ice if you are cautious.

places.name: Aboudi Coffee Break
places.note: Fresh juices including cane and mango in a sit-down setting.

landmarks: Karnak Temple
Egypt's largest temple complex overwhelms with its Great Hypostyle Hall, a forest of 134 colossal papyrus columns raised to Amun-Ra over 1,500 years.
Valley of the Kings
Hidden in desert cliffs, the rock-cut tombs of New Kingdom pharaohs, including Tutankhamun's, blaze with astonishingly preserved paintings of the afterlife.
Luxor Temple
In the city's heart, Amenhotep III and Ramses II's riverside temple is most magical at night, when floodlights gild its colossi and colonnades.
Mortuary Temple of Hatshepsut (Deir el-Bahari)
The female pharaoh's terraced sanctuary rises in dramatic tiers against sheer ochre cliffs, one of the ancient world's most audacious architectural statements.
Medinet Habu (Mortuary Temple of Ramses III)
Arguably the West Bank's most underrated site, this vast temple retains vivid original paint and towering reliefs of Ramses III smiting the Sea Peoples.
Colossi of Memnon
Two shattered 18-meter quartzite giants of Amenhotep III have guarded the West Bank road for 3,400 years, once famed for 'singing' at dawn.
Valley of the Queens
Burial ground of royal wives and princes, it crowns any visit with Nefertari's tomb, whose luminous ceilings rank among ancient Egypt's supreme artworks.
Avenue of Sphinxes
The restored 2.7-kilometer processional way linking Luxor and Karnak temples, lined with hundreds of sphinxes, reopened in 2021 with pharaonic pageantry.
Luxor Museum
Beautifully curated and mercifully compact, this Nile-side museum displays masterpieces including royal mummies and the muscular basalt statue of Thutmose III.
Ramesseum
Ramses II's memorial temple shelters the toppled colossus that inspired Shelley's 'Ozymandias,' its fallen grandeur a poignant meditation on kingly ambition.

train.note: Frequent daytime trains and overnight sleeper services (Watania) run along the Nile from Luxor south to Aswan (~3 hrs) and north to Cairo (~9-10 hrs) and Alexandria; book sleeper berths ahead in the winter high season.

bus.note: Go Bus and Blue Bus run air-conditioned coaches from Luxor to Aswan, Hurghada, the Red Sea coast and Cairo; there are no scheduled international coach services.

ferry.note: Local public ferries and feluccas cross the Nile between the East Bank and the West Bank antiquities throughout the day; there are no international ferry routes.

half.name: Dendera Temple
half.blurb: The remarkably intact Ptolemaic Temple of Hathor with its painted ceilings, crypts and famous zodiac relief, about 1.5 hours north of Luxor.

half.name: Esna (Temple of Khnum)
half.blurb: A sunken, richly carved and recently cleaned temple in a riverside market town an hour south, often paired with the Nile lock.

full.name: Abydos & Dendera
full.blurb: Two of Egypt's finest temples on one long day north—Seti I's Abydos with its King List and the Hathor temple at Dendera.

full.name: Edfu & Kom Ombo Temples
full.blurb: The superbly preserved Temple of Horus at Edfu and the riverside double temple of Kom Ombo, an easy drive south toward Aswan.

full.name: Aswan & Philae Temple
full.blurb: Egypt's serene southern city with the island Temple of Isis at Philae, reachable in about three hours by road or train.
